title: Heir without knowing (Kern ch. 4)
hookLine: the disciples realize they were heirs all along
tomorrow: The rain on the plants (Kern ch. 5)

lines: YOURS, BUT LIVED AS IF NOT.
cards: What do you have that you've never claimed? A skill you treat as a hobby. A family recipe nobody wrote down.

A library card in a drawer. Things can be yours for years while you live as if they belong to someone else. In the Lotus, the disciples have just told of a son who swept the yard of a house that was his.
Now they tell the Buddha who that son was, and it turns out they've been describing themselves the whole time.

teach.b: The disciples say: the rich man is the Buddha, and we are like his sons. Clearing the dirt heap was our practice of clearing away wrong views and bad states. It was real work, and it mattered.
But we were content with the day's wage. The son was glad of his pay and asked for nothing more; in the same way the disciples had reached their own release, their own peace, and called it enough.

They even taught the bodhisattvas about the Buddha's great knowledge, they say, without ever thinking it could be theirs, like the son put in charge of the treasure, who handled it every day and still slept in his hut.
The Buddha knew our narrow wishes, they say, so he did not tell us everything at first.
He worked beside us in plain clothes, so to speak, with teachings we could take in. That's skillful means from chapter two, seen from the receiving end.
And now, in this sutra, the Buddha has called together the whole assembly and told us: you are my children, and what is mine is yours.
In Kern's translation they describe it as a treasure that came to them without their seeking it. They hadn't asked for an inheritance. They hadn't known there was one.
They were never really hired hands.

They were heirs from the start. What changed was not what they owned, but that someone finally said it out loud, and they were ready to hear it. Tomorrow the Buddha answers them with a picture of his own, about rain.

how: Some Lotus Sutra teachers in East Asia read the disciples' explanation in chapter four as a key to the sutra: those on every path are the Buddha's children and heirs, raised by skillful means toward the one vehicle.

o: a child adopted into a rich family who never learns of it
the disciples, who worked for wages, were heirs from the start
a son who inherits a fortune and gives it all away

games.q: heirs all along: tap the pairs.

s: the disciples say their earlier practice was worthless
they compare it to clearing the dirt heap: real work, but they took the wage and stopped there.
the disciples say they taught others about the Buddha's knowledge without thinking it could be theirs
like the son who handled the treasure and still slept in his hut.
the disciples asked the Buddha for their inheritance
they say the treasure came to them without their seeking it.

games.q: you are one of the disciples. you've reached your own peace and you're content. the Buddha says everything he has is yours. what do you say?
o: we never sought this, and it has come to us
we earned this by our hard work
we would rather keep our wage
games.why: they say the treasure came without their seeking it; they had been heirs all along without knowing.

practice: Let your mind go back through the people who gave you something: a grandparent's patience, a teacher's love of a subject, words of a tradition you grew up near.
Let one come forward, and name it plainly to yourself: this is mine; I was given this. Notice, without judging, whether you've been living as if it belonged to someone else.

wordCard.voice: Heir without knowing. The disciples see they worked like hired hands, but were the Buddha's heirs from the start, and the treasure came unasked. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: heir, one who receives a share; in Pali texts, heirs of the dhamma.

carryVoice: Your line: heirs all along. The treasure was never a wage. Rest well.
